issues.legal_issue: A co-holder's plea of acquiring exclusive title by adverse possession does not raise a referable title issue in a statutory partition suit where no limitation period is prescribed for bringing that suit.
material_facts: The claimant and the opposing co-holders had been declared entitled to equal shares in a common agricultural holding.
The claimant brought a statutory suit for partition, and one co-holder opposed it by claiming exclusive possession for more than twelve years and title by adverse possession.
The governing schedule prescribed no limitation period, or starting point for one, for a co-holder's partition suit.
issues.conclusion: The adverse-possession plea was clearly untenable in this partition suit and did not require the revenue court to frame and refer a title issue to the civil court. The appeal was allowed and the order directing a reference was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 13(2) and 55(1) of the Delhi Land Reforms Act, co-holders acquire statutory rights and a co-holder may sue for partition. Sections 185 and 186(1), read with the explanation to section 186(1) and Schedule I, entry 11, govern the revenue court's jurisdiction and referral of a genuine title issue. Because no limitation period is provided for a partition suit, the majority reasoned that a co-holder cannot acquire title by adverse possession against another co-holder so as to defeat that partition claim; the plea is therefore clearly untenable within the explanation to section 186(1). Section 67(d), concerning extinction of a bhumidhar's interest when possession is lost and the right to recover it is time-barred, did not support the opposing co-holder's plea in these circumstances. The majority relied on no earlier cases for this holding.

predicates.adverse_possession_claim_against_coholde: Another co-holder claimed that possession of the common holding had given them exclusive title against the claimant.
predicates.partition_claim_has_no_limitation_period: The governing rules set no limitation period for the co-holder's partition claim.

issues.definition: When a co-holder seeks statutory partition, another co-holder claims adverse possession, and the partition claim has no limitation period, the adverse-possession claim is not referred as a title issue.

issues.legal_issue: A plea of adverse possession between co-holders raises a title issue for referral only when the pleadings set out the essential facts constituting ouster and adverse possession.
material_facts: The opposing co-holder claimed exclusive title by adverse possession in resisting the partition suit.

The written statement did not specifically plead all essential ingredients of ouster, including hostile animus, uninterrupted possession for the required period, and open exercise of exclusive ownership to the knowledge of the other co-holders.
The defence also relied on alleged events predating the creation of the statutory co-holder rights.
issues.conclusion: The written statement did not adequately raise a title issue, so there was no occasion to frame an issue or refer it to the civil court. The concurring judgment agreed that the appeal should be allowed on this ground, while disagreeing that the absence of a limitation period itself made an adverse-possession plea untenable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 186(1) of the Delhi Land Reforms Act requires referral when a question of title is directly and substantially in issue; its explanation excludes a clearly untenable plea intended solely to oust the revenue court's jurisdiction. Section 332 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act was identified as in pari materia. For co-holders, possession is ordinarily treated as possession on behalf of all; adverse possession requires ouster or its equivalent, including hostile animus, long and uninterrupted possession, and open exercise of exclusive ownership to the knowledge of the other co-holder. The concurring judgment relied on Gaya Parshad Dikshit v. Nirmal Chander, Ezaz Ali v. Special Manager, Court of Wards, Maharajadhiraj of Burdhwan v. Subodh Gopal Bose, P. Lakshmi Reddy v. L. Lakshmi Reddy, Mohammad Baqar v. Naim-un-Nisa Bibi, Karbali Begum v. Mohd Sayeed, Coera v. Appuhamy, and Mohd. Zain-ul-Abdin v. Syed Ahmad Mohiuddin. It also relied on Rana Sheo Ambar Singh v. Allahabad Bank for the proposition that statutory landholding rights are newly created rights.
